extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, and students seeking guidance on English grammar and usage
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for correct and clear use of English parts of speech (adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, interjections) and sentence-level syntax, intended to help writers and editors produce idiomatic, unambiguous prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compound adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound adverb consists of two or more words that function together as an adverb; a compound adverb appears to be a single word but is a compound of several words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compound adverbs should be used cautiously and sparingly because they tend to make the tone stuffy. Examples: 'in the meantime', 'for a while', 'here and there'; compound single-word examples: 'notwithstanding', 'heretofore'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial degrees — positive
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive adverbs express a quality without reference to any other thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the nurse spoke softly'; functions like positive adjectives (see related guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming comparative adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative adverbs compare an action by two entities; most one-syllable adverbs not ending in -ly form comparatives with -er (synthetic); multisyllable adverbs usually use more/less (periphrastic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: synthetic 'sooner', 'harder'; periphrastic 'more ineptly', 'less painfully'. Exceptions exist for adverbs where -ly is not a suffix (e.g., 'early'→'earlier').

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming superlative adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Superlative adverbs compare an action across three or more entities; one-syllable non -ly adverbs form superlatives with -est (synthetic); multisyllable adverbs use most/least (periphrastic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: synthetic 'hardest', 'soonest'; periphrastic 'most acutely', 'least wisely'. Superlatives sometimes used loosely for emphasis rather than comparison ('most skillfully').

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A few adverbs have irregular comparative and superlative forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'badly'→'worse'→'worst'; 'little'→'less'→'least'. Use a good dictionary to check irregular forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncomparable adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many adverbs are noncomparable because they are absolute by definition or indicate categories (time, position, number, place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'eternally', 'never', 'singly', 'uniquely', 'universally', and many indicating time ('now', 'then'), position ('on'), number ('first'), place ('here').

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of adverbs (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverb should generally be placed as near as possible to the word it is intended to modify to avoid miscues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example ambiguous: 'the marathoners submitted their applications to compete immediately' — does 'immediately' modify 'compete' or 'submitted'? Put the adverb next to the intended word: 'the marathoners immediately submitted their applications to compete.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs modifying adjectives/adverbs/prepositions/conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an adverb qualifies an adjective, an adverb, a preposition, or a conjunction, it should immediately precede the word qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'our vacation was very short'; 'the flight took too long'; 'your fence is partly over the property line'; 'leave only when the bell rings.' Adverb(s) grouped with an adjective form an 'adjective cluster' (e.g., 'a classically trained pianist').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs modifying intransitive verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: When an adverb qualifies an intransitive verb, it generally follows the verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the students sighed gloomily when homework was assigned'; 'the owl perched precariously on a thin branch'. Exceptions: 'always, never, often, generally, rarely, seldom' may precede the verb ('mountaineers seldom succeed in climbing K2').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs and linking verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs do not generally follow linking verbs; linking verbs connect a descriptive word with the subject, and the descriptive word after the verb applies to the subject, not the verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine if a verb is linking by whether the descriptive word describes an action/condition or the subject. Example: 'the sculptor feels badly' (literal tactile impairment) vs. 'the sculptor feels bad' (predicate adjective describing the subject). Some adverbs that typically precede intransitive verbs may modify linking verbs ('she quickly became uncomfortable'; 'he sometimes seems dishonest').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverb placement within verb phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: When an adverb qualifies a verb phrase, the normal place is between the auxiliary verb and the principal verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the administration has consistently repudiated this view'; 'the reports will soon generate controversy'. Some adverbs may follow the principal verb ('you must go quietly'). There is no strict rule against splitting infinitives; splitting is acceptable for emphasis, clarity, or natural sound ('to boldly go', 'to strongly favor'), but avoid splitting when moving the adverb does not change meaning or sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of preposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A preposition is an uninflected function word or phrase linking a noun element (its object) with another part of the sentence to show relationship (position, direction, time, source, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The object's usually a noun or pronoun in the objective case. Prepositions usually precede their object, with exceptions (e.g., with relative pronoun 'that' or 'which' constructions where preposition may follow the object).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple and compound prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple prepositions consist of a single monosyllabic word; compound prepositions have two or more syllables or words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simple 'as', 'at', 'by'; compound 'into', 'outside', 'upon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrasal (complex) prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrasal prepositions are two or more separate words used as a prepositional unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'according to', 'because of', 'by means of', 'in addition to', 'in spite of', 'with respect to'. Many are symptoms of bureaucratese; prefer a single-word preposition when suitable ('about' instead of 'with regard to').

rubrics_metrics.name: Participial prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial preposition is a participial form functioning as a preposition (or subordinating conjunction) and does not create dangling modifiers when lacking a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'assuming', 'barring', 'concerning', 'considering', 'during', 'notwithstanding', 'owing to', 'provided', 'regarding', 'speaking of'. See guidance on dangling modifiers elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositional phrases — definition and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A prepositional phrase consists of a preposition, its object, and modifiers of the object; it can function as a noun, an adverb (adverbial phrase), or an adjective (adjectival phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: noun use 'for James to change his mind'; adverbial 'we strolled through the glade'; adjectival 'the cathedrals of Paris'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositional function (relationship signaling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepositions signal many relationships such as spatial, time, cause, means, possession, exceptions, support, opposition, and concession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: spatial 'to, from, out of, into'; time 'at, for, throughout, until'; cause 'because of, on account of'; means 'like, with, by'; possession 'without, of'; exceptions 'but for, besides, except'; opposition 'against'; concession 'despite, notwithstanding'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of prepositional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A prepositional phrase with an adverbial or adjectival function should be as close as possible to the word it modifies to avoid awkwardness, ambiguity, or unintended meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating ambiguity: 'Is there a person with a small dog named Sandy here?' (unclear whether person or dog named Sandy) vs. 'Is there a person named Sandy here with a small dog?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinements on placement of prepositional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prepositional phrase equally modifies all elements of a compound construction, it follows the last element; if subject is singular and followed by a plural prepositional phrase, predicate remains singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the date, the place, and the budget for the wedding have been decided' (phrase follows last element); contrast 'the man and his two daughters have arrived' vs. 'the man with two daughters has arrived'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending a sentence with a preposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on terminal prepositions is unnecessary and pedantic; ending a sentence with a preposition is permissible and often more natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'This is the case I told you about' is preferable to overly formal 'This is the case about which I told you.' The old 'rule' was based on a false Latin analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clashing prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid juxtaposed identical prepositions (back-to-back prepositions) that clash, especially when a phrasal verb precedes a prepositional phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example problematic phrasing: 'he gives in in every argument.' Recast to avoid clash: 'rather than continue arguing, he always gives in' or 'in every argument, he gives in.' See also guidance on phrasal verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptical prepositional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some prepositional phrases are elliptical independent expressions that often start a clause and can be detached without affecting meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'for example', 'for instance', 'in any event', 'in a word', 'in the long run'. They are normally detachable from the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun case in prepositional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns appearing in prepositional phrases are usually in the objective case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'with me', 'alongside her', 'between them'. Note: 'than' may function as conjunction or preposition — in formal registers 'taller than I [am]' predominates, while 'taller than me' is common in spoken English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositions and functional variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words can function as prepositions or other parts of speech; the distinguishing feature of a preposition is that it has an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like 'above, behind, below, by, down, in, off, on, up' can be prepositions (take objects) or adverbs (no object). Some conjunctions may serve as prepositions (e.g., 'than', 'but' in 'everyone but Fuzzy').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and misuse of 'like'
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally, 'like' functions adjectivally (governs nouns/noun phrases) and not as a conjunction; as a preposition it takes a noun/object. Its use as a conjunction replacing 'as' or 'as if' is common in speech but has been considered nonstandard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred formal constructions: 'it happened just as I said it would' (not 'just like I said'); 'you're as well known as I am' (nominative after 'as'). Colloquial: 'he ran like he was really scared' is common dialectal usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and misuse of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Only' can function as adjective, adverb, or conjunction and emphasizes the word or phrase that immediately follows it; misplacement commonly causes ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare: 'I bought only tomatoes at the market' (bought nothing else) vs. 'I bought tomatoes only at the market' (bought tomatoes there and nowhere else). In speech, 'I only bought tomatoes' is acceptable due to intonation, but in writing precise placement is important for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overuse of prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepositions are easily overused; stylistically, a good ratio to strive for is one preposition per ten to fifteen words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends five editorial methods to reduce the number of prepositions in a sentence: cutting prepositional phrases, cutting unnecessary prepositions (by avoiding nominalizations), replacing prepositional phrases with adverbs, replacing them with genitives, and using active voice to eliminate 'by' phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting prepositional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: If context permits, eliminate prepositional phrases to tighten prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the most important ingredient in this recipe' can be reduced to 'the most important ingredient' when context makes 'this recipe' clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting unnecessary prepositions (avert nominalizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominalizations (nouns formed from verbs) often require extra prepositions; using the verb instead can eliminate prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'toward maximization of' → 'to maximize' (so 'our efforts toward maximization of profits failed' → 'our efforts to maximize profits failed').

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacing prepositional phrases with adverbs
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong adverb can replace a weaker prepositional phrase to produce more direct prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the president spoke with force' (weak) vs. 'the president spoke forcefully' (stronger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacing prepositional phrases with genitives
rubrics_metrics.description: An of-genitive prepositional phrase can sometimes be replaced with a genitive ('s) construction for concision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the complexity of the street map' → 'the street map's complexity.' See guidance on genitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using active voice to eliminate prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting long passive constructions (which often include 'by') to active voice eliminates prepositional phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the ship was sailed by an experienced crew' → 'an experienced crew sailed the ship.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositional idioms and collocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain verbs, adjectives, and nouns conventionally take specific prepositions; mastery of these idioms is necessary for idiomatic English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides an extensive list of common words with their typical prepositions (e.g., 'abide with/by/none', 'abound in/with', 'accompany (adj.) by', 'accord in/with/to', etc.). Writers should consult such lists and double-check usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifts in prepositional idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepositional idioms can shift over time; there may be differences between traditional literary usage and contemporary usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may choose a preposition for euphony or deliberate denotative/connotative differences (e.g., 'oblivious of' vs. 'oblivious to'; 'smitten with' vs. 'smitten by'). Be aware of register and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjunction is a function word that connects sentences, clauses, or words within a clause; in Standard English, conjunctions connect pronouns in the same case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'and' connecting two sentences; 'but' connecting clauses; 'but' joining two adverbs. Pronoun case following conjunctions like 'than' or 'as' is normally nominative in formal registers ('you are wiser than I [am]').

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple, compound, and phrasal conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions may be simple (single-word), compound (single words formed by combining words like 'although'), or phrasal (multiword connectives like 'as though', 'provided that').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize class for correct syntactic behavior and punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinating conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinating conjunctions join words or groups of equal grammatical rank and can be copulative, adversative, disjunctive, or final; they may be single words or correlative pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'are you speaking to him or to me?'; 'the results are disappointing but not discouraging.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlative conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlative conjunctions are paired conjunctions that must frame structurally identical sentence parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'both...and', 'either...or', 'not only...but also'. Ensure parallel structure: 'she wanted both to win the gold medal and to set a new record'; 'they not only read the book but also saw the movie.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinating conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinating conjunctions introduce clauses that are dependent on an independent clause and denote relationships like time, reason, condition, purpose, place, manner, comparison, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'until', 'because', 'if', 'when', 'so that'. Beware that a pure subordinating conjunction has no antecedent and is not a pronoun or adverb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special uses of subordinating conjunctions (relation types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinating conjunctions often denote nine types of relationships: comparison/degree, time, condition/assumption, reason/concession, purpose/result, place, manner, appositions, indirect questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are provided for each relation type (e.g., comparison: 'than', 'as'; time: 'since', 'after'; condition: 'if', 'unless'; reason: 'because', 'since'; purpose: 'so that', 'in order that'; manner: 'as if', 'as though'; indirect questions: 'whether', 'why').

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbial conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverbial conjunction connects two clauses and also qualifies a verb; they may be relative (with an antecedent) or interrogative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: relative adverbial conjunctions like 'where' (with antecedent 'café' in 'that café where we first met'); interrogative adverbial conjunctions like 'when', 'why' in indirect questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning a sentence with a conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a sentence with conjunctions such as 'and' or 'but' is not grammatically incorrect and is common in high-quality writing; however, use 'but' only when the idea truly contrasts with the preceding one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the contrasting force—if 'and' can be substituted, 'but' may be wrong. 'But' is effective to introduce a paragraph developing a contrary idea. Historical objections to sentence-initial conjunctions are baseless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning a sentence with 'however'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'However' can begin a sentence but is more ponderous and less impactful than 'but'; it's often more effective within a sentence to emphasize the preceding phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example within-sentence use: 'The job seemed exciting at first. Soon, however, it turned out to be exceedingly dull.' 'However' used in the sense 'in whatever way' is acceptable without a following comma: 'however that may be.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctions and verb number
rubrics_metrics.description: Some conjunctions affect whether a verb should be plural or singular: 'and' and 'through' impart plurality; 'or' and 'either-or' distinguish elements and may require singular verbs if elements are singular; other conjunctions may have no effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the best vacation and the worst vacation of my life were on cruises' (plural); 'a squirrel or a chipmunk raids the bird feeder every day' (singular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and punctuation of interjections
rubrics_metrics.description: An interjection or exclamation denotes strong feeling and has little or no grammatical function; it may stand alone as a sentence; punctuation distinguishes meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Oh! I've lost my wallet!'; 'Ouch! I think my ankle is sprained!'. Introductory words like 'well' and 'why' can act as interjections when used as meaningless utterances ('well, I tried my best'). See punctuation guidance (6.34, 6.35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interjections
rubrics_metrics.description: Interjections are natural in speech and frequently used in dialogue; as midsentence interrupters they can direct attention or reflect attitude, especially in informal tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'because our business proposal was, ahem, poorly presented, our budget will not be increased this year.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Interjections and functional variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because interjections are grammatically independent, parts of speech normally serving other functions can be used as interjections (exclamatory noun, adjective, verb, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'good!' (adjective), 'idiot!' (noun), 'help!' (verb), 'indeed!' (adverb), 'me!' (pronoun), 'and!' (conjunction), 'quickly!' (adverb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words used exclusively as interjections
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words function only as interjections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: 'ouch', 'whew', 'ugh', 'psst', 'oops'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax denotes the rules governing how words are arranged into sentences; in analytic languages like English, word order is particularly important for expressing meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that word order indicates grammatical relations in English (subject before verb for declaratives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement (declarative) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sentences are statements with a declarative structure in which the clause contains a subject and the subject precedes the verb; sometimes the subject is implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to idioms where the subject may follow part of the verb phrase in certain negative constructions ('scarcely had we arrived when...').
